title: Service Signal Catalog and Incident Orchestration Guide
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview:

This document defines the Service Signal Catalog (SSC) — a compact, actionable mapping of monitoring signals to incident impact classes, initial on-call actions, and orchestration templates. It also includes an incident orchestration checklist tailored for SLO degradations, short runbook snippets for common failure modes, an escalation matrix, a lightweight game‑day plan, and status page templates for both internal and customer communication.

Why this exists:
- Reduce cognitive load during the first 15 minutes of an incident by standardizing what a signal means and the immediate next steps.
- Improve time-to-detection and reduce MTTx (mean time to X) by ensuring signals are triaged consistently.
- Provide templates for concise, accurate customer communications.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: on-call engineers, incident commanders, SRE leads, product incident liaisons, and customer success for high-impact incidents.
- Scope: Production-facing Redwood services (hosted API, routing layer, runtime), dashboards, alerting, and public status page communications. Not intended for task-level developer debugging notes.

1) Service Signal Catalog (SSC) — quick reference table

| Signal name | Source/Tool | Symptom example | Initial impact class | Default responder | First 5-minute action |
|-------------|-------------|-----------------|----------------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| token-inflight-queue-depth | metrics (Prometheus) | queue > 500/host for 2m | P2 latency spike | routing-service oncall | 1) Scale pool if autoscale failed; 2) Check routing backpressure logs; 3) Post incident-start on #ops-incidents |
| kv-cache-miss-rate | metrics + trace | miss rate > 30% | P3 cost increase / tail-latency | runtime-inference team | 1) Validate cache node health; 2) Re-enable fallback cache; 3) Record metric trend in incident doc |
| model-disk-read-errors | logs (Elasticsearch) | IO errors reading model shards | P1 degradation (requests fail) | runtime-inference oncall | 1) Failover model hosting to replica; 2) Open storage incident runbook; 3) Notify Incident Commander |
| rate-limit-error-500 | logs + API gateway | spike in 500s across routes | P1 outage | api-gateway oncall | 1) Confirm if auth or quota system is root cause; 2) Put temporary throttling exemptions for customer-critical routes; 3) Update status page |
| region-db-replica-lag | monitoring | replica lag > 30s | P2 partial outage | infra-database oncall | 1) Promote replica if safe; 2) Repoint read traffic; 3) Validate writes to primary |

Notes on using the SSC:
- Impact classes: P1 (functional outage or severe user impact), P2 (degraded but usable), P3 (cost/perf regression), P4 (informational). Use the impact class to choose the comm cadence and stakeholders.
- Default responder is the team roster entry for primary ownership; if unavailable, follow escalation matrix below.

2) Incident orchestration checklist — first 20 minutes (SLO degradation focus)

Immediate (0–5 minutes):
1. Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty and set incident channel (e.g., #inc-<service>-<YYYYMMDD>-<short>).
2. Incident Commander (IC) assigned: person with IC role in rotation (if none, senior oncall takes IC).
3. Post initial incident summary: service, signal, estimated impact, region, and slack link.
4. Determine and log impact class (P1/P2/P3/P4).

Primary triage (5–15 minutes):
1. IC confirms who will triage network/infra, runtime, and routing.
2. Run the targeted checks from SSC for the signal observed (example commands below).
3. If SLO (latency or availability) is degrading, set immediate mitigation target: rollback, failover, or capacity increase.
4. Create a short-term mitigation plan (15–60 minute window) and communicate ETA to stakeholders.

Stabilize and communicate (15–60 minutes):
1. Apply mitigation (configuration rollback, scaled replicas, model variant fallback).
2. Verify mitigation by observing targeted SLO metrics and user requests.
3. Update internal status and, if impact> P3, prepare public status page message.
4. If mitigation fails, escalate to oncall lead and consider customer notifications.

3) Runbook snippets and useful commands

A. Check routing queue depth (CLI):

# Check recent queue depth for routing service
redwoodctl metrics query "token_inflight_queue_depth{service=\"routing\"}" --window 5m --step 15s

B. Failover model host (short form):

# Promote replica and rotate traffic
redwoodctl runtime promote-replica --service runtime-models --replica-id r-02 --dry-run=false
redwoodctl routing set-weight --service model-pool --replica r-02 --weight 100

C. Quick latency snapshot (tracing + p99):

# Query tracing service for top spans
obsctl traces query --service api-gateway --top-spans --window 10m --output table

D. Temporary customer-exempt throttling (api-gateway):

# Add exemption for customer <tenant-id>
api-gwctl exemptions add --tenant <tenant-id> --duration 30m --reason "incident mitigation"

Include these snippets in longer runbooks; they are intended as copy-paste actions for initial mitigation. Ensure to record all CLI actions in the incident timeline.

4) Escalation matrix and contact rules

- If no acknowledgement within 3 minutes from primary responder, PagerDuty escalates to team lead.
- If incident not mitigated within 30 minutes and impact class is P1/P2, paging to SRE Director and Product Incident Lead.
- If customer-facing SLA breach is likely (projected >1 hour to remediate), Customer Success and Legal are notified immediately by IC.

Escalation ladder (simplified):
1. Primary oncall -> 3 minutes -> team lead
2. Team lead -> 30 minutes -> oncall lead / SRE manager
3. SRE manager -> 60 minutes -> Director of SRE + Product Incident Lead
4. Director -> 120 minutes -> CTO and Head of Customer Success (for P1)

5) Status page and customer comm templates

Internal status update (first public/internal post):
- Title: Ongoing disruption: <service> (<region>)
- Body: We are investigating elevated error rates for <service> in <region>. We have identified <signal> as the initial indicator. Current impact: <short description: e.g., increased latency affecting 10% of requests>. Mitigation actions underway: <e.g., rerouting traffic to healthy pools, promoting model replicas>. Next update: <time in minutes>

Customer-friendly status page release (short):
- Summary: We are aware of issues affecting <service> in <region> and are actively investigating.
- Current impact: Some customers may see increased latency or failures for API calls.
- What we are doing: Routing traffic away from affected hosts and enabling fallbacks to maintain availability.
- ETA: We expect a mitigation within approximately <30–60 minutes>. We will post more updates as we have confirmed progress.

Post-incident follow-up template (to publish when incident resolved):
- Summary: Incident affecting <service> caused by <root cause summary>. Start: <time>. End: <time>. Impact: <users affected / SLOs violated>.
- Timeline: Key events (alert, mitigation steps, rollback, verified recovery).
- Root cause: <concise technical root cause>.
- Changes: Immediate remediation and long-term action items with owners and due dates.

6) Roles and responsibilities (oncall rotation playbook highlights)

- Incident Commander (IC): Runs the incident, posts updates, decides severity and customer notifications.
- Primary Responder / Triage Owner: Investigates signal source, executes mitigations.
- Communications Lead: Writes and posts status page and customer messages; coordinates with CS.
- Infrastructure Lead: Manages failover and capacity changes.
- Postmortem Owner: Drafts the postmortem within 72 hours and collects action items.

Rotation guidance:
- Primary oncall shifts are 1 week for SRE and 1 week for runtime teams; IC role is assigned per-incident (not per shift) and is typically the most senior engineer on shift who volunteers or is nominated.
- Handoffs: 15-minute overlap for shift handovers; outgoing oncall must list active incidents and any stale alerts suppressed.

7) Game day scenarios and checklist (quarterly exercise)

Objective: Validate detection, comms, orchestration playbooks, and failover paths.

Scenario A — Cross-region latency regression:
- Signal injected: synthetic clients show p95 latency spike in eu-west-1 only.
- Expected run: routing team shifts traffic, runtime team validates model replicas, IC practices status update cadence.
- Metrics to validate: p95 latency, error rate, rate of failover.

Scenario B — Cache cascade and cost spike:
- Signal injected: KV cache miss rate increases to 60% causing cost and tail latency rise.
- Expected run: runtime team toggles cache tiering, SRE observes cost metrics, comms posts an internal blameless recap.

Game day checklist:
1. Create a temporary incident channel and assign roles.
2. Execute SSC steps for the triggered signal.
3. Run mitigation and measure recovery time.
4. Record timeline and evaluate whether communication cadence met expectations.
5. Post-game summary and action items within 48 hours.

8) Postmortem and continuous improvement rules

- A blameless postmortem is required for any P1 or P2 incident where SLOs missed, or customer-impacting issues lasted > 30 minutes.
- Postmortem must include: title, summary, timeline (15-minute granularity), root cause analysis, remediation, and action owners with target dates.
- Postmortem review: scheduled with SRE + product + CS within 7 days. Action items tracked in the incident tracker board.

9) Governance and runbook lifecycle

- Runbook reviews: every 6 months or after any incident that used the runbook. Owner updates the runbook and records changes in the runbook change log.
- Decommissioning signals: if a metric turns noisy (false-positive rate > 20% for 30 days), retire or retune the alert after cross-team agreement.
